Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

We wish to compute ${K}^{′}(t),$ where

$$
K(t)={\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
{K}^{′}(t)={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂t}[({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})^{2}]\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})^{2}] & =2({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3}) \\  & =2({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\cdot 3{t}^{2} \\  & =6{t}^{2}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6{t}^{2}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{t}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+{t}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{1}^{2}+{t}^{3}x{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}+{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{′}(t) & =6{t}^{2}(\frac{7}{3}+{t}^{3}) \\  & =2{t}^{2}(3{t}^{3}+7).\end{aligned}
$$
